notes.meaning: The northern regions of Zebulun and Naphtali were the first to suffer invasion and defeat under the Assyrians. God allowed this border land to be humbled in judgment, but He promised that the area around the Sea of Galilee would later receive great honor. This began to come true when Jesus lived and preached there, bringing hope to a despised corner of the country.

People trapped in spiritual blindness and deep suffering are pictured as walking in pitch darkness and living under death's shadow. God promised that a brilliant light would dawn on them when the Messiah arrived to bring truth and life. The prophet speaks as if this rescue has already occurred, showing how completely certain God's promises are.

God causes His people to grow and fills them with overflowing joy. Their celebration is compared to farmers gathering in a bountiful harvest or soldiers happily dividing the goods won after battle. Because their joy comes from God's presence, it is a lasting and holy gladness.

God shatters the heavy wooden yoke and the beating rod that cruel oppressors had placed on the people's shoulders. This victory is compared to Gideon's defeat of the Midianites, where God won with a tiny, unarmed band rather than human might. In the same way, the Messiah frees His people from the cruel bondage of sin and the devil by divine power.

Every heavy boot used in battle and every bloodstained uniform is thrown into the fire as fuel. The warfare has ended so completely that weapons and soldier equipment are no longer needed. This points to the unbroken peace the Messiah establishes when He puts an end to all hostile powers.

The foundation for all this peace is a baby boy given by God to save His people. He is truly human as an infant born into the world, yet truly divine, carrying the entire burden of government upon His shoulders. His names show who He is: a Wonder of a Counselor filled with divine wisdom, the Mighty God, the eternal Fatherly protector of His people, and the Prince of Peace.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars view these titles as royal praise for an earthly Davidic king acting as God's representative in battle, with their full divine meaning realized only later in Jesus.

notes.meaning: The Messiah's peaceful rule will continually expand and never come to an end. He sits on King David's throne to establish an everlasting kingdom based on fairness and right living. God's own passionate love and burning commitment to His honor guarantee that every part of this promise will come to pass.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe the throne of David refers to a future thousand-year earthly reign of Christ from Jerusalem before the eternal state.

notes.meaning: God sent a prophetic message of warning against Jacob, and it struck the northern kingdom of Israel. God faithfully warns His people before He sends punishment so they have opportunity to turn back to Him. Because God's word never fails, this judgment was as good as done.

All the northern tribes, especially the leaders in the capital city of Samaria, would feel the reality of God's word. Instead of being humbled by their early troubles, they responded with proud and stubborn hearts. Because they refused to listen to God's prophet, they would have to learn through bitter experience.

The people boasted that they could easily overcome any setback through their own strength. If their humble houses of sun-dried brick were knocked down, they bragged they would rebuild with costly cut stone; if common sycamore trees were cut down, they would replace them with fine cedars. They treated God's discipline as nothing and dared Him to do worse.

Because Israel proudly brushed off God's correction, the Lord stirred up fierce enemies against them. The Assyrians, who had conquered Israel's ally Syria, would now turn their armies against Israel. God was lining up these hostile nations to bring down Israel's false confidence.

Enemies attacked from every direction: Syrians pressed in from the east, and Philistines struck from the west, devouring the land like wild beasts. Yet even after all this ruin, God's holy anger did not subside. His hand remained raised to strike again because the people still refused to repent.

The tragedy of the nation was that trouble did not lead them back to God. The Lord had struck them so they would turn away from their sins, but they refused to seek Him. When discipline fails to soften a person's heart, only greater sorrow can follow.

Because the people remained stubborn, the Lord determined to cut off the nation's leadership in a single day. The prophet describes society using two word pictures: head and tail, and tall palm branch and lowly marsh reed. High and low alike would fall together when God's judgment struck.

The prophet explains his figures of speech clearly so no one can miss the point. The elders and respected magistrates are the head guiding the country, while the deceitful prophets are the tail that flatters the people. A teacher who claims to speak for God while telling lies to please the crowd is considered the lowest and most dangerous kind of guide.

The leaders whose job was to guide the nation along the right path instead led them straight into sin. The citizens who followed their bad examples and false promises were completely ruined. When the blind lead the blind, both fall into destruction together.

Corruption had penetrated so deeply into society that even those normally pitied—young men, fatherless children, and widows—would not escape judgment. God usually shows special tenderness to widows and orphans, but here the whole community had turned godless and profane. Because wickedness infected everyone, God's hand stayed raised to strike them again.

Sin spreads through a nation just like a wild forest fire. It starts by burning up dry briars and thorns, and soon sweeps through the thickest woods, sending up huge towers of smoke. God's anger uses the people's own wicked deeds as the fuel that brings them down.

The Lord's righteous anger scorches the country, and the people themselves become fuel for the flames. Order collapses so completely that people show no pity even to their own family members. When people turn their backs on God, normal human love and kindness quickly disappear.

The people claw and steal on every side to feed their greed, yet they are never satisfied. The civil fighting becomes so brutal that it is like people chewing on their own arms, destroying their own relatives and neighbors for food. Selfishness turns a society against itself until it starves from the inside out.

Brother tribes Manasseh and Ephraim, both descended from Joseph, fought each other in bitter civil war. The only matter they could agree on was their common hatred of the southern kingdom of Judah. Yet despite all this self-inflicted misery, they still refused to repent, so God's hand remained lifted to punish them further.
